title: Danny Robins and The Witch Farm cast on dramatising "one of the greatest real-life ghost stories of all time"
excerpt: A new drama inspired by the BBC podcast of the same name
content:
Published: 17 November 2026

The Witch Farm is a new ghost story and mystery set in the Welsh countryside. The drama is inspired by first-hand accounts, theories and real events explored in Danny Robins’ original BBC podcast of the same name.

South Wales, 1989. Bill, Liz and Bill’s teenage son Jonathan leave London for Heol Fanog, a remote farmhouse in the foothills of the Brecon Beacons, determined to make a fresh start. At first the isolation feels like freedom, but when frightening, inexplicable things begin to happen around the house and a strange figure appears the family starts to feel increasingly scared.

  • Watch The Witch Farm on BBC iPlayer and add to your Watchlist

What follows is a steady escalation of the chillingly uncanny - unexplained disturbances and an unsettling sense that they are not alone.

As Bill and Liz begin to investigate the house draws them deeper into a history that refuses to stay buried. And as the land yields its secrets, so too does their marriage - testing their limits of trust, belief, and what they’re willing to deny in order to survive.

The Witch Farm (4x60’) is written and created by Danny Robins (creator of hit BBC paranormal podcast and TV series Uncanny, docu-drama podcast The Battersea Poltergeist and the West End play turned global phenomenon 2:22 - A Ghost Story), directed by Stacey Gregg, and produced by Megan Ott. The executive producers are Simon Barnard, Stacey Gregg and Danny Robins, James Gandhi and Damien Timmer for Mammoth Screen, and Nawfal Faizullah and Rebecca Ferguson for the BBC. Mammoth Screen’s Creative Director Rebecca Keane has overseen the development of the series. Additional funding support has been provided by the Welsh Government via Creative Wales. The series is produced in association with and distributed internationally by ITV Studios. The original podcast was a Bafflegab and Uncanny Media production for BBC Radio 4.

The Witch Farm was filmed on location in Wales.

Coming to BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from Sunday 22 November.

Interviews 

Interview with Danny Robins

Writer, creator and executive producer

How did The Witch Farm come about?

The Witch Farm came out of a podcast that I made for the BBC called The Battersea Poltergeist, another real-life ghost story. It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel. I read about this couple, Liz and Bill Rich, who'd had this terrifying experience in the remote Brecon Beacons in Wales. The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm.

Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary. Once again, it was a big hit and the question was, what next? Telling the story again as a documentary on television didn't feel right, but dramatising it and turning it into a different beast absolutely did!

What can you tell us about the development from podcast to TV drama? 

We took the original story from the podcast as inspiration, in the way that great horror movies are often inspired by first-hand accounts and then grow in the retelling. Now, The Witch Farm as a TV drama has become an even more thrilling ride. The story from the podcast has grown through this new iteration and become something I think will really surprise people.

It's a supernatural thriller that plays out in four parts, a high-octane roller-coaster through a strange chapter in this family's life where they move to what they think is their dream home in this idyllic part of Wales… and it is the absolute opposite. It becomes truly nightmarish, but it goes beyond being a typical ‘haunted house’ story. The family is tested and all manner of secrets and lies emerge. It's as much about their journey as a family as the story of the haunting itself. It culminates in something mind-blowingly scary, which I think will have viewers gripping the edge of their seats.

How do you approach your writing when the story is inspired by real-life people?

Doing a series like this inspired by a real person’s story is an interesting challenge because you want to be true to their experience. It's been incredibly important to us that Liz herself is involved in the process - she was a huge part of the podcast, and she's been an important part of this TV drama as well. I don't want Liz to watch the series and feel it's not leaning into the truth of her story, so I’m in touch with her and her family regularly. That's been our North Star throughout all of this, staying true to Liz and her story. The story has grown as a TV drama. It’s an adaptation, and ‘inspired by’ rather than literally ‘based on’, but I believe everything is grounded in the emotional truth of Liz's story. I think it's scarier for that reason.

The things that terrify me the most are the ones that feel the most real. When people watch the series and see these things happen to a couple like Liz and Bill, in a recognisably normal house, I think they’ll consider how it could happen to them too – that's far scarier to me than CGI demons.

How has it felt for you to see the series be brought to life by the production team? 

One of the greatest pleasures for anybody writing a drama like The Witch Farm is seeing it come to life around you - it’s been a magical journey. In this case, we literally built the house on a soundstage in Wales, a two-story house, fully brought to life. We also had an on-location house in the Welsh countryside for our exterior scenes.

When you're on a set, you imagine it’s going to feel fake. You knock on a fake wall or turn a tap that doesn’t work, but everything worked and was real. There was a stone floor, brick walls, the taps flowed, the electricity worked. It was a proper house; you could have lived there.

How does the series differ from Liz’ personal experiences and the podcast?

If you have listened to The Witch Farm podcast before, watching the series will feel very fresh and very different. I've never been interested in rehashing things. Like with my series Uncanny, where the TV version is totally different, new stories to the podcast, the live shows and the books, it was important to me to move on, develop, adapt and grow The Witch Farm for the TV drama. Viewers will see things they recognise from the podcast, but also a lot of new things with the story going in interesting directions. It's an entirely new beast, I think, and all the more exciting for it.

What did Wales bring to the series as a setting?

This is such a Welsh story, it was so important to us to have a real Welsh accent to everything we did. Gabrielle Creevy who plays Liz is Welsh, and she brings absolute authenticity to the role. Our crew was almost entirely Welsh. It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales. We also have a brilliant theme tune by CATTY, a fantastic up-and-coming Welsh artist. It’s the absolute perfect title track for this show!

The Brecon Beacons is a landscape unlike any other. Until you go there, it's quite hard to appreciate just how strange, alien, beautiful and wonderful it is. You can understand how a family could arrive there and feel like they were landing on the moon. It's a place where silence feels like a sound, where there is a profundity to the absence of people there, somewhere you can feel swallowed up by nature.

At first in our story the family revel in it, they love the isolation and the fact they've escaped the city and they can do what they want. But then, if you're somewhere like that, nobody can hear you scream and suddenly it becomes a place that can be alive with threat and where escape is much harder…

What do you hope viewers feel when they watch the series?

I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it. It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast. It’s particularly moving towards the end as we shift through the gears of this story.

I hope viewers will laugh a little as well. As in all my work, humour has always been important. I think a contrast of light and darkness is needed when dealing with serious events.

Also, hardwired into everything I've done has been that debate between belief and scepticism – do ghosts exist? Every ghost story is always a ‘choose-your-own-adventure’ situation –you can sit there and enjoy it as a howdunnit’ in terms of the human story, wondering whether psychological or environmental factors brought the family to this state – or you can enjoy it as a ‘whodunit’ and try to work out who the ghost is.

What’s crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions. But I think there will be a little finger of terror working its way down your spine, raising those hairs and sending a bit of a shiver. This really is one of the greatest real-life ghost stories of all time and I feel very privileged to be dramatising it. Prepared to be spooked!

Interview with Gabrielle Creevy (Liz)

What drew you to The Witch Farm?

I've always wanted to do a horror, and The Witch Farm is both a horror and a psychological thriller, which felt like something I hadn't seen on TV before. When I did my research and listened to the podcast on which it’s based, I thought it was very interesting.

I loved the scripts and they're scary, whilst also having an emotional arc in them - there's always something to keep you on your toes.

The story is inspired by real events and first-hand accounts, what was it like bringing that to the screen?

What we've done is tell a version of the story. I'm not playing the real Liz, I'm playing a version of her for the world we've created. But it's always scary because you want to do a good job for the real people and you want them to be happy - I met her and she's lovely!

Have you ever experienced anything supernatural, and has working on the show changed your opinion on things of that nature?

I don't think I have. I’ve probably thought I had and then it was just someone downstairs moving. I'm kind of in the middle, I do think there is something, but I don't know what it is. I don't think I'll ever know either. I'm not going to think too much about it because I'll spiral and I'll start to think, ‘oh my God, am I real? Do I exist?’ So, I'm not going to go there.

How would you summarise the story of The Witch Farm?

The Witch Farm is about a family who, at the point we meet them, have moved to the Brecon Beacons and have found a house in the countryside; there's loads of space and they think it's going to be a fresh start. Then they start to experience supernatural things…

Where do we meet Liz at the start of the series?

Liz is a very strong woman. At the beginning of the story, she's with Bill and his son from a previous relationship, and she’s pregnant. Liz and Bill met a few years earlier and they just want a fresh start away from London. She thinks maybe moving to the countryside in Wales is going to help and change things for her family.

Liz's journey throughout the show is a messy one and it's really difficult as she’s having to deal with Bill’s issues. She’s very family-orientated, she wants to keep everything and everyone together. She's in the middle; she wants to sort out what is happening in the house, but also in their marriage.

What was it like working with your co-stars Michael Socha and Lewin Lloyd?

Michael brings everything to the role of Bill, he's such a fantastic actor. I was thrilled when I found out I was going to work with him. He's a very natural actor, so easy to act alongside. When I watched him at work I was taken aback - Michael brings real emotional depth to him.

Lewin's fantastic too. The role of Jonathan is a tricky part because he's also going through his own stuff. Lewin would bring these great ideas to a scene and it was obvious he’d put a lot of thought into it. Lewin has an intensity to the way he brings a character to life.

Do you have a favourite scene?

I enjoyed my scenes with Michael because I didn’t know what I was going to get, he's so good at bringing something different to a scene, which was always fun.

How does filming a supernatural story compare to acting in other dramas?

I love horror films and going to the cinema to see them. I always think how difficult they must be to make. When you're making one it's hard because you're just talking to the wall some of the time, or you're imagining things. But those scenes were fun because our crew did cool things with lighting and camera movements, our director Stacey Gregg really had a vision for that. Michael and I had some tricky scenes where our characters were terrified and emotional, we needed to map out the journey of their relationship in those moments and Stacey was always good at listening to us and adapting.

What was it like filming in Wales?

I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same.

How did the set and design help bring the story to life?

This is probably one of the best sets I've been on, the attention to detail is so great. I don't know whether it was intentional, but the bedroom just felt damp. The colour palette, the wallpaper and the way it fades in places, just from looking at the set it felt cold and sad. There are little extra details in there like in the props, but I don't want to spoil anything. As the series goes on through each episode you start to feel like the house is getting colder, sadder and more miserable as the family become trapped there.

How do you think viewers will react to the series?

I hope they understand how it wasn't as easy for this family to get out of the house as people might think. When you hear about this story you might say ‘they could have just moved’, but it's not always that simple. This is a horror and a thriller, so I hope the audience do feel that fear at times - there are a few jump scares - but I hope they enjoy it too!

Interview with Michael Socha (Bill)

What drew you to The Witch Farm?

I'm always a little wary of ghostly, horror stories because I'm a bit sceptical at first. But when I read the scripts, I realised the character of Bill was ultimately going through a really hard time and I enjoy playing those sort of roles.

Were you aware of this story before you read the script?

I'd never heard of the story but I've got a lot of Welsh friends and when I explained I was working on something called The Witch Farm about a haunted house in the Brecon Beacons, it seemed like a popular story here.

What were your first impressions of the scripts?

Initially I was given the first two episodes, I loved the family dynamic and the slow introduction of a ghostly element. The decline of Bill and the family unit was what I found most interesting. I was looking forward to getting into episodes three and four to see exactly how things would go and also how the darkness, both mentally and in terms of the haunting, would progress.

How would you summarise the story of The Witch Farm?

I'd say it's a ghost story, essentially, but it's also a story of a family coming together in crisis. In terms of Bill, he is an artist and he made a bit of a name for himself in London. He's carrying some baggage and trying to escape things that happened in his past. He is slowly deteriorating on many levels for many different reasons. I think he ultimately blames himself for a lot of the goings-on in the haunted house and he eventually loses it.

What was it like filming the supernatural scenes?

I've worked on a couple of supernatural projects before and as an actor you have to believe that what's going on is really happening. I often try and draw on my own experiences, but I've never really had any supernatural ones apart from when I was younger… I used to sleep eat and I'd go downstairs at my mum's house and help myself to food. One night I went down to the fridge, and I thought I heard a voice say my name… I ran as fast as I could back to my bed. The next day, my sister asked, what happened last night? I said, what do you mean…? Turns out she was the one saying my name, she was just stood at the back door having a cigarette and I’d thought it was a ghost!

It can sometimes be quite difficult to portray a realistic emotion for things you haven’t experienced, but I was working with a great bunch of people. We had an amazing crew, director and the art department on this were incredible, which made the job a lot easier. I think your environment helps when working with odd, supernatural things.

Has working on the series changed your views on the supernatural in any way?

I'm quite sceptical, but I'm working with people who have had supernatural experiences and I'm open-minded enough to consider the possibility. As filming went on, I reconsidered things – just because I haven't experienced the supernatural, doesn't mean these things haven't really happened for other people. I'm still a sceptic, but I'm definitely not calling anybody a liar!

What was it like filming in Wales?

I think I've filmed in Wales more than any other place in the world. I've got a lot of good friends in Wales and I always have great fun here, the crews are always amazing. Wales is really close to my heart, it's incredible, beautiful, and it's got everything – cities, the sea, mountains and greenery.

Interview with Lewin Lloyd (Jonathan)

What drew you to this role?

I immediately connected with the director, Stacey Gregg. We had a conversation and they shared their love for the character of Jonathan – or Johnny. I could instantly tell that this show was in the right hands with them as the director. Also, I wanted to do a horror project, I've never done anything like this before.

Were you aware of this story before reading the script?

No, I'd never heard about it before but I did some research after getting the role and it sounds like a horrific experience, to say the least. I could draw most of inspiration from the script because that’s the story we're telling..

What were your first impressions of the script?

When I first read the scripts, it was all in one sitting. I just had to find out what happened next straight away and I was surprised at every direction that it went in. Hopefully the audience will feel the same way when they watch it.

How would you summarise the story of The Witch Farm?

The Witch Farm is about a family from London who move out to the Welsh countryside in the late 80s. Shortly after moving into a new place, they realise that not everything is how it seems - their house has a dark history and it's haunted. We explore how the family deal with it and how it affects them.

What can you tell us about your role?

Jonathan, or Johnny, is a 16-year-old boy at the start of the series when we first meet him. I think he's already dealing with a lot in his head straight off the bat and now he's been dragged to live in the middle of nowhere in Wales with his new young step-mum and his dad. There's definitely an adjustment to be made there. But I think despite that, what Johnny really does want underneath everything is a loving family who are there for him. Having said that, he does like to use his voice and he's not afraid to speak out - that's something I like about him.

How does it feel to be portraying a story inspired by real events and first-hand accounts?

I didn’t really think too much about that during filming. I took the script our writer Danny Robins created and grew the character from there – whilst also developing it with our director, Stacey.

How did you find working with your co-stars, Gabrielle Creevy and Michael Socha?

Gabby is the leading lady of the show and I think she carries that brilliantly. What I love about her interpretation of Liz is that there’s a vulnerability there, but you can also see her fierceness and her determination to protect her family, which is really nice. I like the motherly nature she gives her character.

Michael brings a lot of power and energy to the role of Bill. I think you can watch the character and like him, then feel sorry for him, maybe even hate him at some points. There's clearly a lot of nuance and complexity in that performance. I also really like how Michael understands the relationship between Johnny and Bill. They’re father and son but there's a slight disconnect there.

What was it like filming the supernatural scenes? 

The supernatural scenes were always fun to film. I do like the conversational, normal scenes which show character dynamics, but in the supernatural ones as an actor, you really have to ask, what is Johnny thinking in this moment? How would Johnny react to this? Because it is so far from reality.

It was cool seeing all the brilliant actors in full costume, hair and make-up, they looked terrifying sometimes. You're watching them peering behind a corner or hiding in the shadows of the corner of my room, that's already creepy enough. It helped you get into a character straightaway.

Have you ever experienced anything supernatural yourself?

I've never experienced anything supernatural. I've never had an interaction with a ghost or anything like that. I'm not sure what I believe in, but I just know that I want to keep it as far away from me as possible. I don't want anything to do with it. I think we're all grateful on set that nothing spooky happened because we were kind of expecting it at the start, but I don't think anything happened.

Has working on this series changed your views on the supernatural in any way?

I feel like I'm more open to the fact that there could be something out there. Danny (Robins) said that this story specifically is one which makes people consider if there could be such a thing as ghosts. I'm not sure where I stand on it.

What can you tell us about the sets that were created for the series?

The set for the interior of the family home is great. There's such an attention to detail it really feels like a lived-in house. They built this long dark creepy hallway which I had to walk down and act scared. The floorboards were creaking and there was nobody around me, so it already felt a little bit scary - it was perfect.

What was your favourite scene to film? 

One of my favourite scenes to film was when a dream sequence in the ruins. I had to fall off this pretty high ledge so underneath my t-shirt I had a full harness on. I just had to completely trust the stunt coordinators behind me, and they were brilliant. It's a weird feeling letting your body completely relax, drop and then getting caught at a midway point in the air. But it was fun, it made me feel like I could do all my own stunts after that. I'd like to do more stuff like that, definitely.

What makes The Witch Farm a unique series to watch?

I think The Witch Farm is something that grabs your attention straight away and doesn't let it go. It's really tense and thrilling.

What do you hope audiences will feel when they watch the series?

I hope the audiences feel terrified when they watch it, that's the aim.

Interview with Sian Gibson (Bethan)

What drew you to this role?

I really wanted to be part of The Witch Farm because I'd already listened to the podcast and I was aware of the story. I'm very into the supernatural; I love anything to do with that. When the script came through, I was beyond excited. I knew the ending, but there's so many twists and turns it was such a great read. The plot is really grounded in the family as well, it doesn't just focus on the spooky bits. It's a real emotional rollercoaster and a family drama - that really brings it down to earth, so the sceptics can’t say it's just a silly ghost story. I'm not a sceptic, I truly believe.

How would you summarise the plot of The Witch Farm?

At the centre of the story are Liz and Bill, a young couple who move to Wales to live in this beautiful, secluded farmhouse called Heol Fanog. But things aren't as they seem and it goes a bit spooky, there's lots of paranormal activity. The story explores troubles in their relationship as well.

What can you tell us about the role of Bethan?

Bethan works at the local mother and baby group, that’s where Liz meets her. Bethan is a warm, friendly character, a pillar of the community. She's also very spiritual and has joined a spiritualist church. She takes Liz under her wing and convinces her that she can connect with the ‘other side’. Bethan thinks she could speak to whatever it is that's in the house and tell it to leave the family alone. She's there to help Bill and Liz but whether she does or not… you'll have to watch. Bethan is a lovely character, her heart is in the right place, but Bill isn't so sure and he makes that quite clear.

Did you enjoy filming in Wales?

I love filming in Wales. I am Welsh and I live there, so it's great to film where I'm from. The Witch Farm is so uniquely Welsh in its tone, it really fits in with the moody landscapes. It looks absolutely beautiful but it's also a little bit eerie, dark and bleak.

What did the sets bring to the series?

The set is unbelievable; everything looks so real. It's got this cold, dark, damp quality to it, and it's huge. The set designers have done such a good job. I think it's so unique and I've not seen anything like it.

What was your favourite scene to film?

I really loved filming the séance, I’d love to go to a real one. I don't know how good Bethan was at it… but I enjoyed that scene, it was great.

What was it like filming the supernatural scenes?

I was so excited to do the séance, but also a bit nervous because I've never done anything like that. Stacey (Gregg), the director, created a lovely atmosphere but also it felt incredibly spooky as well. It was quite easy to get into it because we had lights flickering and noises, there was lots to react to. But it was also incredibly funny and quite hard to get through without laughing because everything was so heightened. It's not something you do every day, is it?

Have you ever experienced anything supernatural?

Never, and I would never want to experience anything supernatural because I'd never sleep again. I would hate it. But I truly believe and I really want there to be something there, I just never want to see it. I’ve got a bit of an obsession with clairvoyance and going to see mediums to speak to the other side. They've varied in success, but I'm still hoping. If I ever saw anything, I don't know what I'd do.

What do you hope audiences will feel when they watch the series?

I hope audiences will be a little bit scared. They'll want to keep coming back for more because there's so many different twists and turns. It keeps it all exciting and no one knows which way it's going to go. They'll love seeing Wales looking absolutely stunning and beautiful. They'll just love the spooky supernatural element and the fact it's something different, I don't think there's anything else like it.
